ordinance.text: This ordinance applies to any organised foot race held wholly or partly on a public street or public path in the City.
A race's crowd means its expected runners plus its expected spectators. A crowd over 800 is a large crowd.
A hot date is a race date in June, July or August.
The permit fee must be paid when the application is filed.

The application form must state the organiser, event type, event date, expected runners, venue, a description, the route details (road closure, arterial road, count of major crossings) and the distance to the nearest hospital. An incomplete form is returned to the applicant.
A street race may be held only from 1 March to 30 November.
The Events Office considers traffic conflict for any race that closes a road.
The Events Office considers crowd pressure for any race with a crowd of 300 or more.
The Events Office considers medical emergency for every race.
Every race must hold event liability insurance, shown by a certificate of insurance that names the organiser and the venue, covers the race date, and has a limit of at least $1,000,000.
A certificate that has expired by the race date, or that names another venue, does not meet ORD-7.1.
Proof must be an attached document of a type the evidence steward has listed. A statement in the form or in a cover letter is not proof.
An attached document of a type the steward has not listed goes to an officer, who decides the case. The steward then decides whether to list it.
A document that disagrees with the application, for example by naming another date, goes to an officer.
An application must name every road that the race closes.
A race that closes a road must file a traffic plan. The plan must cover every closure on the route, control at each major crossing, signed diversions, and a way through for emergency vehicles.
In reviewing a race, the Events Office takes into account whether the route uses an arterial road.
A race that closes a road should have a police escort, confirmed in writing by the police in a letter or an email.
A route with three or more major road crossings is a route with many major crossings. The Events Office may take this into account.

A race with a crowd of 300 or more must file a crowd plan. The plan must cover marked spectator areas with their capacities, a staged start, stewards in stated numbers and positions, exit routes, and who can stop the race.
In reviewing a race, the Events Office takes into account whether its venue is too confined for people to spread out. The race plan must give enough detail to judge this.

Every race must file a medical plan. The plan must cover staffed first aid positions, water and rules for extreme weather, a named receiving hospital with a transfer route, medical communications, and a named qualified lead.
A race should have an ambulance on site under an agreement with an ambulance provider.
A hospital more than 10 km from the race is a far hospital.
In reviewing a race, the Events Office takes into account whether it falls on a hot date.
A race that passes every check and whose assessed risk is below the lower threshold may be approved without an officer.
A race whose assessed risk is at or above the lower threshold is decided by an officer.
The policy owner may set a stop switch. While it is on, every case that passes the basic checks goes to an officer.
A race whose highest assessed severity reaches the ceiling is decided by an officer, however small its likelihood.
If any automated step fails, the case goes to an officer.
A denial is proposed with the clause it relies on, and an officer signs it.

evidence_types.name: Certificate of insurance
evidence_types.claim: The organiser holds event liability insurance in force on the race date at the race venue.

evidence_types.name: Police escort letter
evidence_types.claim: The police have committed to escort this race on the race date.

evidence_types.name: Police escort email
evidence_types.claim: The police have committed to escort this race on the race date.

evidence_types.name: Ambulance agreement
evidence_types.claim: An ambulance provider has committed to keep an ambulance on site for this race on the race date.

evidence_types.name: Race plan
evidence_types.claim: The document describes the course and its dimensions.

evidence_types.name: Traffic plan
evidence_types.claim: The document describes how traffic is managed for the race.

evidence_types.name: Crowd plan
evidence_types.claim: The document describes how the crowd is managed for the race.

evidence_types.name: Medical plan
evidence_types.claim: The document describes medical cover for the race.

does_not_count.what: A statement in the form or in a cover letter that the event is insured
does_not_count.reason: The form and cover letter are the applicant's own claims and are never sources of proof.

does_not_count.what: A report by the applicant of a verbal promise from the police or an ambulance provider
does_not_count.reason: A commitment must be in the provider's own document.

settings.why: The share of automatic approvals the city accepts being labelled risky.
settings.if_raised: More events are approved automatically, and risky approvals may rise.

settings.why: The share of high-risk cases that must really be labelled risky before the system calls them high risk.
settings.if_raised: Fewer cases are marked high risk, and more fall into the review band.

settings.why: A case whose highest severity reaches this value always goes to an officer, because the product of likelihood and severity can hide a rare catastrophe.
settings.if_raised: Fewer cases go to an officer on severity alone, and a rare catastrophe is more likely to be approved automatically.

settings.why: Lets the policy owner send every case that passes basic checks to an officer.
settings.if_raised: Turning it on stops all automatic approvals until it is turned off.

settings.why: The numbers that stand for rare, possible and likely. They are policy values, not measurements.
settings.if_raised: Every case's risk rises, and thresholds must be chosen again.

settings.why: The numbers that stand for minor, serious and critical. They are policy values, not measurements.
settings.if_raised: Every case's risk rises, more cases reach the ceiling, and thresholds must be chosen again.

settings.why: How much old counts on a leaf keep their weight when a correction reaches that leaf.
settings.if_raised: Old counts fade more slowly, so each correction changes less.

settings.why: How many officer reviews pass before thresholds are chosen again during the replay.
settings.if_raised: Thresholds follow the weights less often, so the curve moves in larger steps.

settings.why: A tree is flagged when its mean leaf entropy is the highest of all trees and above this value, which points to a missing question.
settings.if_raised: Fewer trees are flagged, and a missing question is more likely to go unnoticed.

settings.why: The answer an evidence question takes when a record is supported.
settings.if_raised: A supported document counts for more, and risk falls on cases that have one.

settings.why: The answer an evidence question takes when a record is unsupported or absent.
settings.if_raised: A missing document counts against a case less, and risk falls on cases without one.

settings.why: The answer an evidence question takes when a record is contradicted.
settings.if_raised: A contradicted document counts against a case less.

settings.why: How many pseudo-cases the first guess is worth on each leaf.
settings.if_raised: Training and corrections move the first guess more slowly.

settings.why: How many passes training makes over the labelled cases.
settings.if_raised: Training takes longer and settles closer to the labels.

settings.why: How often the officer agrees with the label when the run uses simulated answers instead of the LLM officer.
settings.if_raised: The simulated officer makes fewer wrong corrections, and the curve looks better than a real officer may manage.

settings.why: The Jev version whose answers are pinned for this run. A returned model that differs counts as a failure.
settings.if_raised: Changing the version changes the stored-answer key, so every case is read again.

settings.why: How many model requests run at once. TypeSafe's cookbook reports rate limits on a shared key at 8.
settings.if_raised: Reads finish sooner, and rate limits become more likely.

settings.why: The total spend at which a run stops.
settings.if_raised: A run may spend more before it stops.

settings.why: The total Jev input at which a run stops. Reset after the first 5 cases are measured.
settings.if_raised: A run may send Jev more before it stops.

settings.why: How many real cases run before the project owner looks at the cost and the output.
settings.if_raised: More money is spent before the project owner's first look.

settings.why: If the total projected at the first stop is above this, the project owner reconsiders the model or effort.
settings.if_raised: A costlier projection passes without a second look.

hazards.name: Crowd pressure
hazards.description: People gather more densely than the space allows, at the start, along the course or at the finish.

hazards.name: Medical emergency
hazards.description: A runner or spectator needs urgent care during the race.

hazards.name: Traffic conflict
hazards.description: Runners and traffic meet, or a closed road blocks other traffic.
